title: Question 6

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Fig. 6.2 shows the variation of $V$ with the charge $Q$ on the plates of capacitor $C$ as the capacitor discharges.
{{figure:figure_6_2}}
parts.text: Show that the energy stored in capacitor $C$ at time $t = 0$ is $1.8\text{ mJ}$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 6.2 with V on one axis and Q on the other. Think about building up charge on a capacitor little by little and what multiplying a small p.d. by a small charge tells you.
Hint 2: Read the charge $Q$ when $V = 8.0\text{ V}$ from the straight line, convert $\mu\text{C}$ to $\text{C}$, then find the area of the triangle under the line.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why area means energy**
Think of charging in tiny steps. Moving a tiny charge $\Delta Q$ across a p.d. $V$ needs work $V \Delta Q$. Adding up all those little rectangles gives the total work, which is the area under the $V$ against $Q$ graph. Because the line starts at the origin, the shape is a triangle.

Step 2: **Read the starting values and calculate**
At $t=0$ the capacitor is fully charged to $$V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$$ From Fig. 6.2 the corresponding charge is $$Q_0 = 450\,\mu\text{C} = 450 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$$ Area of triangle: $$E = \frac{1}{2} \times Q_0 \times V_0$$ $$E = \frac{1}{2} \times 450 \times 10^{-6} \times 8.0 = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$$ That is $1.8\text{ mJ}$, as required.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the capacitance of capacitor $C$. Give a unit with your answer.
hints: Hint 1: You now know the charge on the plates and the p.d. across them at $t=0$. Recall how capacitance links charge stored to p.d. applied.
Hint 2: Use $Q = 450\,\mu\text{C}$ and $V = 8.0\text{ V}$ with consistent SI units to get $C$ in farads.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Q, V and C**
Capacitance tells you how much charge is stored per volt: $$C = \frac{Q}{V}$$ You can read $Q$ and $V$ straight from Fig. 6.2. Equivalently the gradient of the $V$-$Q$ line is $1/C$.

Step 2: **Put numbers in**
$$Q_0 = 450 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}, \quad V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$$ $$C = \frac{450 \times 10^{-6}}{8.0} = 5.6 \times 10^{-5}\text{ F}$$ So about $56\,\mu\text{F}$. The unit is the farad, $\text{F}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Fig. 6.3 shows the variation with $t$ of $-\ln\left(\frac{V}{8.0\text{ V}}\right)$.
{{figure:figure_6_3}}
parts.text: Show that, when $t$ is equal to one time constant, the value of $-\ln\left(\frac{V}{8.0\text{ V}}\right)$ is equal to 1.0.

markscheme_points.text: V = V0 exp (-t / RC) and τ = RC
V = V0 exp (-t / τ) V0 = 8.0 V, and at one time constant, t = τ V / 8.0 = exp (-τ / τ), so ln (V / 8.0) = -1.0 or -ln (V / 8.0) = 1.0

hints: Hint 1: Start from how p.d. falls during discharge through a resistor. Remember the exponential law involves $V_0$, $t$, $R$ and $C$, and that $RC$ has a special name.
Hint 2: Set $t$ equal to that $RC$ combination and take natural logs of both sides to isolate $-\ln(V/V_0)$. Recall $V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$ here.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write the discharge equation**
For discharge through resistor $R$: $$V = V_0 e^{-t/RC}$$ Here the starting p.d. is $$V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$$ The product $RC$ controls how fast the decay is and is called the time constant: $$\tau = RC$$ So you can write more simply: $$V = V_0 e^{-t/\tau}$$

Step 2: **Put t = tau and take logs**
When $t = \tau$: $$\frac{V}{V_0} = e^{-\tau/\tau} = e^{-1}$$ With $V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$: $$\frac{V}{8.0} = e^{-1}$$ Take natural log: $$\ln\left(\frac{V}{8.0}\right) = -1$$ Multiply by $-1$: $$-\ln\left(\frac{V}{8.0}\right) = 1.0$$ That is exactly what Fig. 6.3 plots on its vertical axis.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the time constant $\tau$ of the circuit in Fig. 6.1.

markscheme_points.text: [t read from graph at -ln (V / 8.0) = 1.0]: τ = 3.2 s

hints: Hint 1: From the last result, one time constant corresponds to a vertical-axis value of 1.0 on Fig. 6.3. Find 1.0 on that axis and read across to the line then down to $t$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read tau from the straight line**
You have shown $t = \tau$ gives $-\ln(V/8.0) = 1.0$. On Fig. 6.3 go up to $1.0$ on the vertical axis, across to the line, then down to the $t$-axis. This gives: $$\tau \approx 3.2\text{ s}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: You now have $\tau$ from the discharge graph and $C$ from part (a). Recall how $\tau$, $R$ and $C$ are linked for a capacitor-resistor circuit.
Hint 2: Rearrange to make $R$ the subject and substitute $\tau \approx 3.2\text{ s}$ and $C \approx 5.6 \times 10^{-5}\text{ F}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use tau = RC**
The time constant combines both components: $$\tau = RC$$ So resistance is: $$R = \frac{\tau}{C}$$ A larger $R$ or larger $C$ makes discharge slower, which makes sense.

Step 2: **Calculate R**
$$R = \frac{3.2}{5.6 \times 10^{-5}}$$ $$R \approx 5.7 \times 10^{4}\,\Omega$$ That is about $57\text{ k}\Omega$.
